notes.japanese: 暗い電燈の下の卓《テーブル》
notes.problem: Doubled word reads as a typo, not as the author's repetition, and stops an English reader at the opening tableau.
notes.sureness: Certain; a check of the Japanese for a single 暗い would settle it.

notes.japanese: その顔にはまだ少しの皺もよってなかった
notes.problem: Wrong preposition and number for English; no writer puts a wrinkle in the singular face.
notes.span: had yet a single wrinkle in the face
notes.suggestion: had not yet a single wrinkle on their faces
notes.sureness: Sure on the English; the faithful reader can confirm number is not meaningful in Japanese.

notes.japanese: その子供のすべてに瞳を注いだ。
notes.problem: Literal rendering of an idiom; English eyes are not poured, so the tender looking turns grotesque.
notes.span: they poured their eyes upon all that was the child
notes.sureness: Sure this is translationese, unsure of the best verb that keeps 注いだ; faithful note should decide.

notes.japanese: 顔一ぱいな微笑《ほゝゑみ》を持って、子供のまるくつき出た頬を指で一寸つまみながら
notes.problem: Grammar collapses so the face seems to do the pinching; has to be read twice to parse.
notes.span: with a face full of smile pinched the round jutting cheek lightly with his fingers
notes.sureness: Certain it is ungrammatical as it stands; how to recast is for the desk.

notes.japanese: ごた〳〵した騒がしさの為に
notes.problem: Cluttering is the wrong English word for noisy clatter and sounds like a machine habit rather than a kitchen.
notes.sureness: Fairly sure; need the faithful reader to confirm the Japanese is sound-noise, not mess.

notes.japanese: あわたゞしく大きな口を開けた、彼は彼自身の口のなかに御飯を押し込んだ。
notes.problem: A large mouth opened and rice pushed makes him sound monstrous, not hurried; no English writer phrases a bite that way.
notes.span: he opened a large mouth hastily, and pushed rice into his own mouth
notes.suggestion: he opened his mouth wide and shovelled rice in
notes.sureness: Sure on the English effect; faithful side to confirm no grotesque is intended.

notes.japanese: かゝはりのない冷やかな不味《まづ》さ
notes.problem: Unconnected leaves an English reader with nothing to taste; it reads as a dictionary word, not a mouthful.
notes.sureness: Fairly sure this is literal stiffness, though unsure what relation かゝはり denies; faithful note would settle it.

notes.problem: Literal version of an idiom that has no meaning in English; hands with nothing to do stops the domestic beat.
notes.span: as if with nothing to do with his hands
notes.suggestion: at a loose end, not knowing what to do with his hands
notes.sureness: Sure this is a set-phrase rendered word-for-word; any native phrasing of idleness would do.

data.say: Supper business is vivid when left alone, but literal wordings stop the English reader cold in eight places; otherwise clean.
